26.text: Cases are by no means rare, however, where the husband, enamored of

27.text: the second wife, becomes indifferent towards the first, and even expels her

28.text: from the house. Precisely such a case is described in a very popular tale,

30.text: “There lived a man with two wives, an old one and a young one. When he took the young

31.text: wife, he abandoned the old one, did not love her nor sleep with her any longer. He beat her all

32.text: the time. In great grief she went out into the desert and came to a bear’s haunt. She entered.

33.text: The bear mother was angry at her for entering. The woman said, ‘Why don’t you kill me?

34.text: My husband always beats me. It is better that you kill me.’

35.text: “The woman stays with the bears and lives with them. When spring comes, the bears let

36.text: her go, with presents and incantations. She returns home, and by means of their incantations

37.text: succeeds in regaining the favor of her husband, and persuades him to drive her rival from the

38.text: house. The latter perishes from hunger and cold.”

39.text: I took down several versions of this tale. I was always anxious to

40.text: ascertain whether jealousy existed to any extent among the Chukchee wives

41.text: of a single husband. When questioned by me on that point, the women would

42.text: generally answer, “We don’t care, we don’t think about those things;” and,

43.text: more definitely, “Good and clever women don’t get angry over such matters.”
